examples.en: Today is the school's founding anniversary, so there are no classes.

examples.ko: 이 대학은 올해 개교 칠십 주년을 맞았어요.
examples.en: This university marks its seventieth anniversary this year.

examples.ko: 개교 이래 처음으로 전교생이 한자리에 모였어요.
examples.en: For the first time since the school opened, all students gathered in one place.

examples.ko: 새 학교 개교를 앞두고 선생님들이 준비하느라 바빠요.
examples.en: Ahead of the new school's opening, the teachers are busy preparing.

examples.ko: 개교가 늦어져서 학생들이 다른 학교에 다니고 있어요.
examples.en: The opening was delayed, so the students are attending another school.

examples.ko: 졸업생들이 개교 때 심은 나무를 구경했어요.
examples.en: The alumni looked at the tree planted when the school opened.

explain: 주로 '개교 기념일', '개교 100주년'처럼 학교의 시작과 관련된 말로 써요. 학교가 문을 연다는 동사는 '개교하다'지만, 말할 때는 '문을 열다', '생기다'가 더 쉬워요. 반대는 '폐교'예요.
explain_en: It is mainly used in expressions about a school's founding, such as '개교 기념일' and '개교 100주년'. The verb form is '개교하다', but in speech '문을 열다' or '생기다' is easier. The opposite is '폐교' (school closure).

examples.ko: 친구가 다음 달에 동네에서 병원을 개원해요.
examples.en: My friend is opening a clinic in the neighborhood next month.
That dental clinic opened last year.
If I become a doctor, I plan to open my own clinic.
It's a newly opened clinic, so the building is clean.
I heard many patients came as soon as it opened.
There's a lot to prepare if you want to open an academy.

explain: '개원하다'는 병원, 학원 같은 곳을 처음 연다는 말이에요. 가게나 식당은 '개업하다'나 '오픈하다'라고 해요. 같은 병원이라도 이미 있는 곳이 문 여는 시간을 말할 때는 '열다'를 써요.
explain_en: 개원하다 is used when a clinic or academy opens for the first time. For shops and restaurants, Koreans say 개업하다 or 오픈하다. When an existing clinic simply opens its doors for the day, people use 열다.

p.n: 개업 is also possible but broader; 개원 is specific to clinics and institutes.

examples.en: Liberation Day is a big celebratory holiday in our country.
On national celebration days, the Korean flag is hung on every street.

examples.ko: 경축일 아침에 가족과 함께 기념식을 봤어요.
examples.en: On the morning of the holiday, I watched the ceremony with my family.
This year's holiday event will be held at the square.
It's a pity that the holiday falls on the weekend.
City hall prepared fireworks to coincide with the holiday.

explain: 국경일처럼 나라나 사회가 함께 기뻐하는 날을 가리키며 뉴스나 안내문에서 써요. 일상 대화에서는 '국경일'이나 '공휴일'이라고 더 자주 말해요.
explain_en: It refers to days the nation celebrates together, like national holidays, and is used in news and notices. In everyday talk people more often say '국경일' or '공휴일'.

examples.en: The child suddenly grabbed my hand.
The puppy snapped up the treat.
It is risky to sign a contract right away just because the terms look good.
He readily accepted my request.
My friend was so happy to see me that she hugged me.

examples.ko: 낯선 사람이 주는 걸 덥석 받지 마세요.
examples.en: Don't just take something a stranger offers you.

explain: 망설이지 않고 갑자기 잡거나 물거나 받아들이는 모습이에요. 손을 잡을 때뿐 아니라 제안이나 선물을 생각 없이 받을 때도 써요. 껴안을 때는 '와락'도 비슷하게 써요.

phrases.example: 좋은 조건이라는 말에 미끼를 덥석 물었다가 후회했어요.
phrases.en: I took the bait right away because the terms sounded good, and I regretted it.
phrases.nuance_ko: 달콤한 말이나 유혹에 깊이 생각하지 않고 넘어갈 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used when someone falls for tempting words or an offer without thinking.

explain_en: It describes grabbing, biting or accepting something suddenly and without hesitation. It is used not only for grabbing a hand but also for taking an offer or gift without thinking. For hugging, '와락' is used in a similar way.

examples.en: I'm hearing all kinds of strange things today.
Stop talking nonsense and let's go quickly.
It's nothing special, so don't worry about it.

examples.ko: 내가 무슨 별소리를 했다고 화를 내요?
examples.en: What did I say that's so bad that you're angry?

examples.ko: 아무도 별소리 안 했는데 혼자 걱정했어요.
examples.en: Nobody said anything in particular, but I worried by myself.
I got scolded for saying all sorts of silly things.

explain: 보통 '별소리 다 한다', '별소리 하지 마'처럼 엉뚱하거나 쓸데없는 말을 들었을 때 써요. 친한 사이에서 하는 말투라 윗사람에게는 조심해야 해요.
explain_en: It is usually used in phrases like '별소리 다 한다' or '별소리 하지 마' when you hear odd or pointless talk. It is casual speech between close people, so be careful with elders.

en: being as swift as an arrow

examples.ko: 그 사람은 신호가 바뀌자마자 쏜살같이 달려갔어요.
examples.en: As soon as the light changed, he dashed off like an arrow.
The vacation flew by in no time.
The puppy saw the ball and came running at lightning speed.
Time flies, and it's already graduation.
The bus passed by at lightning speed.
After getting the call, I rushed to the hospital as fast as I could.

explain: 형용사이지만 대부분 '쏜살같이'라는 형태로 '달려가다, 지나가다' 앞에 써요. 몸의 움직임도, 세월이 빨리 가는 것도 표현할 수 있어요. 시간에 쓸 때는 '세월이 쏜살같다'처럼 조금 문학적인 느낌이 있어요.
explain_en: Although it is an adjective, it mostly appears as '쏜살같이' before verbs like '달려가다' or '지나가다'. It can describe fast movement or time passing quickly. When used for time, as in '세월이 쏜살같다', it sounds a bit literary.

examples.ko: 친구가 어쩌고저쩌고 계속 말하는데 하나도 못 들었어요.
examples.en: My friend kept going blah-blah-blah, and I didn't hear any of it.
Mom nagged me for a while, saying blah-blah-blah about studying.
He just rattled off excuses, yadda-yadda-yadda.

examples.ko: 회의에서 어쩌고저쩌고 얘기가 길었지만 결론은 없었어요.
examples.en: The meeting had a long blah-blah-blah, but there was no conclusion.

examples.ko: 어쩌고저쩌고 말만 많고 행동은 안 해요.
examples.en: He talks a lot, blah-blah-blah, but doesn't act.

examples.ko: 그 애가 나한테 어쩌고저쩌고 하더니 그냥 가 버렸어요.
examples.en: She said something blah-blah-blah to me and just left.

explain: 남이 한 긴 말을 다 옮기기 귀찮을 때 줄여서 흉내 내는 말이에요. '이러쿵저러쿵'과 비슷하지만, 이 말은 들은 말을 대신하는 느낌이 강해요. 격식 있는 글보다 편한 대화에서 써요.
explain_en: People use it to skip over a long speech they don't want to repeat in full. It is similar to '이러쿵저러쿵', but this one feels more like standing in for the words you heard. It fits casual conversation better than formal writing.

examples.ko: 할머니가 저에게 김치 담그는 법을 전수해 주셨어요.
examples.en: My grandmother passed down to me how to make kimchi.
The master craftsman passed his skills on to his apprentice.
I don't hand this secret down to just anyone.
He passed his know-how to his juniors and retired.
There is a school that teaches and preserves traditional dance.
I'm worried because there is nobody to pass the skill on to.

explain: 기술, 비법, 전통처럼 오래 쌓인 것을 한 사람이 다른 사람에게 직접 가르쳐 물려줄 때 써요. 일반 지식을 가르칠 때는 '가르치다'를 써요. '기술 전수', '비법 전수'처럼 명사로도 자주 나와요.
explain_en: Use it when one person directly teaches and hands down long-built things like skills, secret recipes, or traditions. For ordinary knowledge, use '가르치다'. It also appears as a noun in '기술 전수' and '비법 전수'.

en: eve celebration (night before a festival or event)

examples.en: Singers perform at the festival's eve event.
The university's eve festival went on until late at night.
We went to the square to see the eve festival.
The Olympics eve event was broadcast on television.
The roads were jammed because of the eve festival, so I was late.
Friends congratulated me at the pre-wedding eve party.

explain: '전야'는 행사 바로 전날 밤이고, '전야제'는 그날 밤에 미리 여는 작은 축제예요. '축제 전야제', '개막식 전야제'처럼 행사 이름 앞에 붙여 써요. 크리스마스 전날 밤은 '전야제'가 아니라 '크리스마스 이브'라고 해요.
explain_en: '전야' is the night before an event, and a '전야제' is a small celebration held that night. It goes after the event's name, as in '축제 전야제' and '개막식 전야제'. The night before Christmas is not a '전야제' but 'Christmas Eve' (크리스마스 이브).

examples.en: The traffic light turned green.
Cross the road only when the light is green.
This contract is a green light for the business.
My health checkup results came back with a green light.

examples.ko: 수출이 늘어난 건 회복의 청신호라고 봐요.
examples.en: I see the rise in exports as a good sign of recovery.
That news is practically a green light for the team.

explain: 교통 신호의 초록 불을 말하지만, 일이 잘 풀릴 것 같은 좋은 징조라는 비유로 더 자주 써요. 반대말은 '적신호'예요. 신호등 불은 말할 때 '파란불'이라고도 해요.

phrases.en: The new project has gotten the green light.
phrases.nuance_ko: 일이 잘될 것 같다는 좋은 징조가 보일 때 써요. 반대는 '적신호가 켜지다'예요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used when a good sign appears that something will go well. The opposite is '적신호가 켜지다'.

explain_en: It literally means the green traffic light, but it is used even more as a metaphor for a good sign that things will go well. The opposite is '적신호' (red light). In speech, the green traffic light is also called '파란불'.

examples.ko: 그 작가는 올해 새 소설을 출간해요.
examples.en: That author is publishing a new novel this year.
The publisher put out a poetry collection last month.

examples.ko: 저는 내년에 제 첫 책을 출간할 거예요.
examples.en: I'm going to publish my first book next year.

examples.ko: 이 책을 출간한 출판사는 서울에 있어요.
examples.en: The publisher that put out this book is in Seoul.

examples.ko: 신문에 쓴 글을 모아서 책으로 출간하고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to collect my newspaper columns and publish them as a book.

examples.ko: 원고가 늦어져서 아직 책을 출간하지 못했어요.
examples.en: The manuscript is late, so we haven't been able to publish the book yet.

explain: '출판하다'와 거의 같은 뜻이에요. 책을 만드는 쪽이 주어일 때는 '출간하다', 책이 세상에 나왔다고 말할 때는 '출간되다'를 써요.
explain_en: It means almost the same as '출판하다'. Use '출간하다' when the publisher or author is the subject, and '출간되다' when you say a book has come out.

dis.h: a book comes out; neutral, written

p.n: 펴내다 is a native Korean verb with a softer, more literary feel.

examples.ko: 후미진 골목이라 밤에는 혼자 가기 무서워요.
examples.en: It's a secluded alley, so I'm scared to go alone at night.
That restaurant is tucked away, so it's hard to find.
The road is a bit out of the way, but I like that it's quiet.
Even though the shop is tucked away, customers keep coming.
The mountains are secluded and quiet, so they're good for resting.
The neighborhood that used to be tucked away is now very famous.

explain: 길, 골목, 마을처럼 구석진 곳에 써요. '외지다'가 중심에서 멀리 떨어진 느낌이라면, '후미지다'는 으슥하고 안쪽으로 들어간 느낌이 더 강해요. '후미진 골목'처럼 조금 어둡고 쓸쓸한 분위기로 말할 때가 많아요.
explain_en: It describes places tucked into a corner, such as roads, alleys and villages. '외지다' feels far from the center, while '후미지다' feels more shadowy and set back inside. It is often used for a slightly dim, lonely atmosphere, as in '후미진 골목'.
